# Critique of `brand-tokens` — lens: SOUNDNESS AND THE PROGRAMS

Research date: 2026-09-16. Refutation of
[candidate-brand-tokens.md](candidate-brand-tokens.md) under the soundness
lens: P1, P2, P4, P7, P9 and P13 re-derived from the candidate's own §2.4
rule set, against R1–R3, R11, R12, M2(ii), the couplings C1–C18 and the
hazard ladder of MECHANISM-MAP §3. Nothing here selects or rejects a tuple;
it reports what the candidate as written admits, mis-derives or leaves
unstated. Where the candidate's intent is visibly narrower than its rule
text, the finding says so and is still reported, because the rule text is
what a checker would implement.

Method: every rule in §2.4 was read as written (including the direction of
each `⟺`), every derivation line in §3 was re-run against that rule set with
no charitable repair, and each requirement the candidate marks **met** was
tested against the derivation that is supposed to support it. The candidate
declares M8 violated and M4/M6/M7/M9/R5/R8b/R9/R13/R14/R15 partial; a
violation of anything else is undeclared by construction.

---

## 1. Findings

Severity: **fatal** = a ladder hazard is admitted, or a requirement the
candidate marked *met* is violated; **serious** = a program verdict is wrong,
a stated cost is understated, or a needed mechanism is unnamed; **minor** =
wording.

| # | Sev | Program / requirement | Finding | One-sentence fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | fatal | R1(i); P1, P2, P6 | `R-REFINE` is stated as `Pt<ℓ▷e,q,s> ⟺ Pt<ℓ▷e1,q,s1> ⊗ Pt<ℓ▷e2,q,s2>` with a side condition that constrains **only the extents** (`e = e1 ⊎ e2`); `s`, `s1`, `s2` are unrelated, so `Pt<ℓ▷e,W,U> ⟺ Pt<ℓ▷e1,W,I> ⊗ Pt<ℓ▷e2,W,U>` is derivable and `T-READ` then reads uninitialized storage — the step-0 hole read the ladder exists to refuse. `R-CARVE`'s `Pt<ℓ▷e,W,_>` has the same free metavariable. | Add `s = s1 = s2` to `R-REFINE`'s side condition and pin `_` in `R-CARVE`/`R-RETIRE` to a named state, or admit a partial-init state into D3's `s` with a stated join. |
| F2 | fatal | R4 soundness clause, R5(a)(i); P16, P6 | `share` restores the original `W` token "at the construct's end" with no rule that the arms' `R` tokens cannot escape — and P16 explicitly accepts a closure **capturing** `Pt<ℓi▷·,R,I>`, P6 reproduces that capture per iteration. If the closure outlives the construct, an `R` token and the restored `W` token overlap, so §1's load-bearing D4 claim ("the algebra cannot produce two overlapping `W` tokens", therefore holding `W` *is* exclusivity) does not license R4's fact, and R5 ground (i) will admit a write overlapping a live reader. | Make `share` arms closed — the arm's exit context must be exactly its bound token, and a closure capturing a share may not escape the construct — and state the escape rule as part of D2. |
| F3 | fatal | R2; §4.1's own R2 row | `R-CARVE` is written as a biconditional `⟺`. Its backward direction consumes `Deed<ℓ▷e ⇒ ℓ'>` and returns the parent token, with no program event and no `Gone(ℓ')`, so a release obligation is discharged by a ghost rewrite while the run-time block stays allocated: a leak the checker believes was freed, and the arena extent handed back for reuse under a live block. This directly contradicts §4.1 R2's claim that the deed is consumed "only by `R-RETIRE`". | Make `R-CARVE` a one-directional rule (`⊢`, forward only), so the deed can be discharged only by `R-RETIRE`, which is the rule paired with an ending event. |
| F4 | fatal | R1(i), R8a; P13, P3, §2.6 `move` | `R-CARVE` always produces `Pt<ℓ'▷·,W,**U**>` and `R-RETIRE` always produces `Pt<ℓ▷e,W,**U**>`, so no carve/retire round trip can re-expose *initialized* storage. P13's `read(pool[h])` after `compact()` therefore reads a slot token that is `U` and must reject; §2.6's `move` ("R-RETIRE then R-CARVE at the destination") leaves the destination `U`, so a moved struct is unreadable. If the checker silently carries `I` across either rule — the only way the candidate's own verdicts hold — it is a state transition no rule states, and the `U` case is then an admitted hole read. | Add a state-preserving relocation rule (`Pt<ℓ▷e,W,s> ⊢ Pt<ℓ'▷·,W,s> ⊗ Deed`) distinct from allocation's `U`-producing carve, and say which of the two each of `alloc`, `move`, `compact` and slot recycle uses. |
| F5 | fatal | R1(ii), R8a, M2(ii); P13 | `p2 = fixup(Fixup, p)` is claimed to be "a ghost function on location terms, erased; no runtime compare". A compaction moved the object, so the correct `p2` is a **different address**. Erased, `fixup` is the identity and `read(p2)` reads vacated storage — use after relocation, admitted with an accept comment. Not erased, `fixup` is a run-time lookup in a relocation table, which is bookkeeping state the source did not bind, refused by M2(ii). R8a's "contract-visible fixup form" is therefore not supplied, while §4.1 marks R8a **met**. | Drop `fixup` and let `pool[h]` (a source-written handle indirection, which the candidate already accepts) be the only fixup form, and restate R8a's row as met *only* through handle re-derivation. |
| F6 | fatal | R1(ii); P4, P9 | `reserve`'s post-state returns `Eq(backing(ℓv), ℓ')`. `Eq` is an equality on **location terms** with no stated discipline: two `reserve` calls give `Eq(backing(ℓv),ℓ')` and `Eq(backing(ℓv),ℓ'')`, hence `Eq(ℓ',ℓ'')` by transitivity, hence `Pt<ℓ''▷·,W,I>` is a token for the **retired** `ℓ'` — precisely the revival §2.6 and P2 say is impossible. Worse, if `backing(ℓv)` denotes different atoms at different program points then §2.3's central claim ("a multiset of tokens. Nothing else… no per-identity state table") is false: the checker needs a flow-sensitive term→atom environment, which the JOIN rule (multiset equality on *types*) cannot carry across arms. | Make the backing an existentially bound atom with no `Eq` fact (`reserve` returns `∃ℓ'. Pt<ℓ'▷·,W,I> ⊗ Backing(ℓv, ℓ')` as a *linear* rebinding that consumes the old one), and declare that location terms are rigid. |
| F7 | fatal | R1(i), R1(iii); P7, P1 | `T-TAKE`, `T-PUT` and `T-REPL` carry **no** `p : ptr<ℓ,T>` premise, so any `W`/`I` token licenses a take through any pointer; and no rule in §2.4 relates the *place* an access names to the token's extent `e`, so `Pt<ℓ▷.f,R,I>` licenses `read(p)` of the whole `T`, and `T-WRITE` sets the whole extent `e` to `I` for a write that touched one field. P1 line 207 and P7 both silently assume a place-to-extent bridge that the vocabulary of §2.1 does not contain. | Add `place(·)` to §2.1 (`p` plus an access path normalizes to `ℓ▷e`), put the pointer premise on all five term rules, and require `place ⊑ e` on read/take and `place = e` on the `I` conclusion of write/put. |
| F8 | fatal | R7 (marked met), C6 | §1 claims C6 ("state as a term over captured conditions") is "**Not needed** … the single largest simplification the tuple buys". Every assigned program refutes it: P1's extent `[0..n)` must track the *run-time value* `len(v)` and its `k≠i ∧ k≠j` refine is discharged against a captured branch condition; P2's `alloc` contract names concrete offsets `o1,o2,o3` that are the arena metadata's run-time content; P4 needs `len < cap`; P13 needs "the current generation is `g+1`". None of these facts has a stated source, and `alloc`'s interface cannot be written without one, so R7 ("a declaration whose entry condition is syntactically unsatisfiable … is rejected at the declaration") is violated at the first allocator, undeclared. | State the value-dependence explicitly — extents may mention ghost-tracked contents of a storage, discharged against a captured path context — and re-price C6, M8 and M10 with it included rather than declaring it eliminated. |
| S1 | serious | P2 `par { fill(b1) \| fill(b2) \| fill(b3) }` | The overlap accept is not derivable. Across `alloc`'s signature the offsets are existentially bound, so the caller holds `In(ℓ1 ⊑ ℓS▷[o1..o1+64))` and `In(ℓ2 ⊑ ℓS▷[o2..o2+64))` with nothing relating `o1` and `o2`; two existential packages give no disjointness. The one route that *does* work — the blocks were carved from disjoint remainders, so they are disjoint by construction — is explicitly disclaimed by the candidate as "NOT by inequality of the names ℓ1, ℓ2 (R4 b)". That is a misreading: R4(b) bars *name inequality*, not a proved disjointness relation over the containment structure, which carve provenance is. | Admit carve provenance as the disjointness derivation (it is a relation over `In` facts, exactly what R4(b) asks for) and drop the offset-arithmetic story. |
| S2 | serious | P1 `push(v, x)` after `put_back` | Accept is wrong on the candidate's own arithmetic: the held token is `Pt<ℓb▷[0..n),W,I>` where `n` is the length, while `push` is said to need `Pt<ℓb▷·,W,I>` **whole** — and the capacity tail `[n..cap)` is `U`, so a whole-extent `I` token over the backing is unobtainable at any point in the program. P1's Γ also never contains the header token `Pt<ℓv▷·,W,I>` that `push` must read `len`/`cap` through. | Restate `push`'s contract over `Pt<ℓb▷[0..len),W,I> ⊗ Pt<ℓb▷[len..cap),W,U> ⊗ Pt<ℓv▷·,W,I>` and carry the header token in P1's Γ. |
| S3 | serious | M1, M4; §2.9's "0 per read" | The elision rule ("the token argument is elided wherever exactly one token of the required type is in scope") is not well defined once one location carries several extent tokens, which is the normal case the moment anything is split — P1 holds three tokens on `ℓb`. The "required type" is `∃e ⊒ place. Pt<ℓ▷e,q,I>`, so argument recovery is a **search over the multiset coupled to a proof obligation** (choosing `[i]` fails, choosing the remainder succeeds only after `k≠i ∧ k≠j` is discharged). Acceptance then depends on the search order unless that order is specified, which it is not; M1 is marked met and M4 is priced as "one token mention per access", both on the assumption the search does not exist. | Specify elision as a total function (most-specific containing extent, ties rejected with a diagnostic) and re-derive M1 and M4's costs from it. |
| S4 | serious | M1, M10 | The extent algebra's cost is understated. `[0..n) ⊖ [i] ⊖ [j]` with symbolic `i`, `j`, `n` needs a canonical form modulo commutativity of `⊖` and, for coverage, a case split on the symbolic order of `i` and `j`; that is a decision procedure over a linear-arithmetic fragment with case analysis, not "a fixed normalizer" costing "O(k²) atom comparisons per location". The fragment is never pinned, so M1's "specification-fixed, deterministic, terminating" is asserted, not shown. | Pin the index fragment and its normal form by grammar, state the decision procedure and its degree, and move M10's row from met to provisional until the degree is measured. |
| S5 | serious | P9, M6(iii) | The caller's `match origin(r) { ℓx => … \| ℓy => … }` is called "a GHOST match, two arms, erased". Erasure is only sound if every arm lowers to identical code; the model states no such obligation, so `{ ℓx => free(x) \| ℓy => read(y) }` type-checks and has no meaning after erasure. The candidate also never says how a non-singleton origin set survives being **stored** in a struct or carried around a loop, which is where P4's cursor and P3's links live. | Require all arms of an origin match to be operationally identical (a syntactic check), and state the origin-set rule for stored and loop-carried pointers or record it as unsupported. |
| S6 | serious | R2, R3 | `R-RETIRE` consumes `Pt<ℓ'▷·,W,_>` with no clause about the **contents**. The token vocabulary `⟨extent, share, init⟩` cannot express "the contents carry no obligation", so freeing a block whose storage holds a linear or affine value with a release obligation is admitted, and the R3 "used twice / never released" diagnostic split does not reach inside storage. | Require `s = U` on `R-RETIRE` (the storage must be emptied by `take` first), which is also what makes §2.6's `free` row honest. |
| S7 | serious | P7 | `free ℓA` is not derivable from the stated context: `Γ = { Pt<ℓA▷·,W,I> }` never contained a `Deed<… ⇒ ℓA>`, and `R-RETIRE` requires one. The derivation's Γ is therefore not the Γ an accepted program would have, and the scope-exit leak check (§2.6, last row) never runs in this program. | Open P7 with `Γ = { Pt<ℓA▷·,W,I>, Deed<ℓH▷e ⇒ ℓA> }` and carry the deed through the derivation. |
| S8 | serious | §2.5 point 2 vs §2.4 | §2.5 justifies `share` as existing for "a call wanting two read tokens for one extent", but §2.4's `share` syntax binds **one** token per arm and arms are alternatives, so two simultaneous read tokens in a single context are not expressible. The stated use case has no construct. | Give `share` a form that binds *n* shares in one context, or withdraw the call-with-two-read-tokens use case. |
| S9 | serious | M5, C2, C16, owner decision 2 | §2.5 point 3 and §4.1 M5 state flatly that "a failed derivation leaves the construct sequential, it never rejects". R5(a) and the owner's interim on decision 2 require **rejection** at a non-erasable construct (spawn/join), and the candidate's own D10 row forces structured fork/join with linear task handles. The blanket fallback silently retunes C2's two exactness directions and C16. | Split the clause: sequential fallback at PAR-1/PAR-2, rejection at spawn/join, and mark M5 partial until a fork/join rule exists. |
| S10 | serious | R4 (marked met) | R4 is marked **met** although its own row's status is *unmeasurable* and its facts are span-shaped ("a storage unwritten over a span", "a loaded value invariant over a span") while a token licenses a point-wise fact. The candidate never argues that no transfer of the token occurred across the span, which is what turns a point fact into a span fact. | Downgrade R4 to partial and add the span argument (the token was not passed to any call between the two points) as an explicit lemma. |
| S11 | serious | R2, R13, M1, M10 | The loop rule is *multiset equality* against the entry context. Any loop that allocates or carves per iteration grows the multiset and is therefore unrepresentable — including P2's arena used in a loop and R13's own accounting hook ("the sum of live deed extents"). The missing mechanism is an iterated/quantified token conjunction with a loop rule that is not equality; D9's row names "quantified element permission" but §2.4 has no rule for it, and M1's "no fixpoint, one pass" claim rests on the omission. | Add an iterated separating conjunction over a loop index with its introduction and elimination rules, and re-state the loop-head rule as equality *modulo* that quantifier. |
| m1 | minor | M7; P8 | `Gone` is COPY and "diagnostic only", and §2.7 licenses dropping it at joins — which removes the payload exactly where P2's and P13's rejections need it. | Keep `Gone` facts at joins; they are copyable, so keeping them costs nothing. |
| m2 | minor | — | `In` is COPY and survives retirement, so stale containments for retired atoms accumulate in Γ and are visible to any disjointness query. | Say that a disjointness derivation ignores `In` facts whose subject is retired. |
| m3 | minor | §2.6 | "the context must be empty of tokens whose deeds are unreturned" is ill-formed: a token has no deed; a deed carries the obligation. | Reword as "the context must contain no `Deed`". |
| m4 | minor | R1(iii) | "stale layout = a layout change carves a fresh atom" names no rule; §2.4 and §2.6 contain no layout-changing operation, so R1(iii)'s sub-property has no derivation and no diagnostic site. | Either add the layout-change event to §2.6's table or mark R1 partial on (iii). |
| m5 | minor | §2.1 vs §2.8 | `Eq` appears in `reserve`'s signature but is absent from §2.1's vocabulary and has no class (copy or linear), so §2.8's "one vocabulary" claim is counted over five ghost forms, not four. | Declare `Eq` in §2.1 or remove it per F6. |
| m6 | minor | §4.2 | The counts table ("met 16") includes R4, R8a, R2, R7, M1 and M2, each overturned or downgraded above; the summary row is the most-cited line of the file and is the one most likely to be read without the derivations. | Recompute §4.2 after the rules are repaired. |

## 2. Program verdicts overturned

Notation follows the ladder: pseudocode with a per-line accept/reject comment
and the rule that produces it. `Γ` is the token multiset. Every line below is
derived from §2.4 and §2.6 as written.

### P1 — candidate says "accepted as required"; **overturned to accepted in part**

```text
v: vec<u64>, len n, cap c;  ℓb = backing(ℓv)
Γ = { Pt<ℓb▷[0..n),W,I> }            // as the candidate states it — and note what
                                     //   is MISSING: no Pt<ℓv▷·,W,I> header token,
                                     //   no Pt<ℓb▷[n..c),W,U> capacity tail
(part_i, part_j) = split(v, i, j)    // accept: R-REFINE twice, i<n, j<n, i≠j
                                     //   — but only if the unstated side condition
                                     //     s = s1 = s2 is added (F1); as written the
                                     //     same rule instance also derives
                                     //     Pt<ℓb▷[0..n),W,U> ⟺ Pt<ℓb▷[i],W,I> ⊗ …
write(part_i, x); write(part_j, y)   // accept: T-WRITE — but T-WRITE sets the WHOLE
                                     //   extent to I with no place premise (F7)
par { write(part_i,x) | write(part_j,y) }
                                     // accept: footprints [i] ⊥ [j], R5(i). STANDS.
read(v[k]), k runtime                // reject, correct verdict, WRONG mechanism:
                                     //   the checker must first CHOOSE which of the
                                     //   three ℓb tokens to elide into the access
                                     //   ([i], [j], or the remainder) and the choice
                                     //   is what decides the verdict (S3)
if k != i && k != j { read(v[k]) }   // accept — and this line refutes §1's C6 row:
                                     //   the R-REFINE side condition is discharged
                                     //   against a CAPTURED BRANCH CONDITION, which
                                     //   is a condition atom the tuple says it does
                                     //   not need (F8)
put_back(part_i, part_j)             // accept: R-REFINE backwards. STANDS.
push(v, x)                           // *** REJECT *** — the candidate says accept.
                                     //   push needs Pt<ℓb▷·,W,I>; the held token is
                                     //   [0..n) and the tail [n..c) is U, so a whole-
                                     //   extent I token over ℓb does not exist at any
                                     //   program point; and push must read len/cap
                                     //   through a Pt<ℓv▷·,W,I> that Γ never had (S2)
push(v, x)  // before put_back        // reject. STANDS, for the stated reason.
```

**Revised verdict:** the two discriminating properties P1 exists to test —
parallel permission for the two element writes, and a diagnostic at `v[k]`
naming the missing fact — both survive. The third, "push must be allowed only
after both are back", does **not**: under the candidate's own extents `push`
is never allowed. The accepted `v[k]` line is derived from a path-condition
mechanism §1 declares unnecessary.

### P2 — candidate says "accepted as required"; **overturned**

```text
arena A: metadata ℓM, byte storage ℓS
Γ = { Pt<ℓM▷·,W,I>, Pt<ℓS▷·,W,U> }
b1 = alloc(A, 64)
  // the contract is written as consuming Pt<ℓS▷[o..o+64),W,U> for a CONCRETE o.
  // Where does the caller get o?  It is the arena's bump offset, a run-time value
  // in ℓM's contents.  The tuple has no vocabulary that relates a token extent to
  // the contents of another storage (F8), so the only writable contract is
  //   alloc : Pt<ℓM▷·,W,I> ⊗ Pt<ℓS▷·,W,U>
  //        -> Pt<ℓM▷·,W,I> ⊗ ∃o,ℓ1. (Pt<ℓ1▷·,W,U> ⊗ Deed<ℓS▷[o..o+64) ⇒ ℓ1>
  //                                   ⊗ In(ℓ1 ⊑ ℓS▷[o..o+64)) ⊗ Pt<ℓS▷·⊖[o..o+64),W,U>)
  // accept, with o EXISTENTIAL
b2 = alloc(A, 64); b3 = alloc(A, 64)  // accept; o2, o3 existential and unrelated to o1
par { fill(b1) | fill(b2) | fill(b3) }
  // *** REJECT *** — the candidate says accept.
  //   The claimed ground is "In(ℓ1 ⊑ ℓS▷[o1..]), In(ℓ2 ⊑ ℓS▷[o2..]) with the extents
  //   proved disjoint".  o1 and o2 are existentially bound at different call sites;
  //   two existential packages prove nothing about each other, so [o1..o1+64) ⊥
  //   [o2..o2+64) is NOT derivable and R5(i) does not fire (S1).
  //   The route that works — ℓ1 and ℓ2 were carved from disjoint remainders of one
  //   parent token, so they are disjoint BY CONSTRUCTION — is the route the candidate
  //   explicitly refuses ("NOT by inequality of the names ℓ1, ℓ2 (R4 b)"), on a
  //   misreading: R4(b) bars name inequality, not a proved relation over containment.
distinct(ℓS, b1)?                    // non-derivable. NEGATIVE TEST STANDS.
free(A, b2)                          // accept: R-RETIRE — but see S6: the rule admits
                                     //   retiring a block whose contents still carry
                                     //   an obligation, since s is `_`
b4 = alloc(A, 32)                    // accept: fresh ℓ4
read(p_into_b2)                      // reject. STANDS, and this is the row's strongest
                                     //   result: address reuse is refused at the TYPE
                                     //   level, before any state is consulted.
free(A,b1); free(A,b3); free(A,b4)   // accept — unless the writer instead applies
                                     //   R-CARVE BACKWARDS, which consumes the Deed
                                     //   and returns the arena extent with no free
                                     //   call at all: the obligation is discharged by
                                     //   a ghost rewrite and the block leaks while the
                                     //   arena hands its bytes to the next alloc (F3)
```

**Revised verdict:** P2's negative test (the refusal of a pointer into `b2`
after `b4` reuses its bytes) is met cleanly and is the candidate's best
result. P2's *positive* overlap requirement ("`fill(b1) ∥ fill(b2) ∥ fill(b3)`
must be permitted to overlap") is **not met**, and R2's "four frees, no
double" is met only if `R-CARVE`'s backward direction is removed.

### P4 — candidate says "accepted with a stated cost"; **overturned to partial with an undeclared hole**

```text
c = Cursor { at: ptr<ℓv,Vec>, i: 0 }   // accept: a pointer in a struct, no token stored
a = c.read()                            // accept
push(v, 5)                              // retires backing(ℓv), mints a fresh atom
b = c.read()                            // reject. STANDS — correct, and it is the row's
                                        //   point: validity is decided by state and
                                        //   proof, not by a borrow that blocks push
if len(v) < cap(v) { push_within(v,5) } else { reserve(v, 2*cap); push_within(v,5) }
b = c.read()
  // *** the candidate's "accept in the then-arm" does not survive where the line is
  //     WRITTEN.  At the join, the then-arm's context holds Pt<backing(ℓv)▷[0],W,I>
  //     and the else-arm holds a token over a FRESH atom.  §2.7 admits the join only
  //     up to existential packing, so the post-join context is ∃ℓ. Pt<ℓ▷[0],W,I> —
  //     and P9's own rule then rejects: "no token is typed at the existential ℓ".
  //     The read is accepted only if the writer DUPLICATES it into the then-arm,
  //     which is a second copy of the branch, not the one the candidate priced.
reserve's ensures: ∃ℓ'. Pt<ℓ'▷·,W,I> ⊗ Eq(backing(ℓv), ℓ')
  // *** REJECT the rule ***
  //   call reserve twice:  Eq(backing(ℓv),ℓ') and Eq(backing(ℓv),ℓ'')
  //   congruence:          Eq(ℓ',ℓ'')
  //   substitute:          Pt<ℓ''▷·,W,I>  is a token for ℓ', which is RETIRED
  //   read through the old interior pointer: ACCEPTED.  Use after free (F6).
free(v); c.read()                       // reject forever. STANDS.
```

**Revised verdict:** P4's required property is "validity decided by state and
proof, not by a borrow that blocks `push`", and on the unconditional `push`
that holds. The conditional shape the candidate offers as the repair is
mis-derived (the accept is inside the arm, not after the join), and the
`reserve` contract that makes the repair expressible admits a use-after-free.
W2's stated cost ("`push` splits into two") is understated: it is "`push`
splits into two **and** every use of the survivor is duplicated per arm".

### P7 — candidate says "accepted as required"; **overturned to underivable as written**

```text
p, q : ptr<ℓA, T>
Γ = { Pt<ℓA▷·,W,I> }                 // the deed is missing from the start (S7)
v = take(p)
  // accept — but T-TAKE is written `Pt<ℓ▷e,W,I> ⊢ take(p) : T ⊗ Pt<ℓ▷e,W,U>` with
  // NO premise `p : ptr<ℓ,T>` (F7).  As written, a take through a pointer to ℓB is
  // licensed by a token for ℓA, and ℓB's hole is never recorded — the step-0 hazard.
read(q)                               // reject: s = U. STANDS, and correctly for the
                                      //   reason the row exists to test: the state is
                                      //   indexed by ℓ and no pointer appears in it.
put(q, move v)                        // accept — same missing premise on T-PUT
read(p)                               // accept. STANDS.
old = replace(p, new); read(q)        // accept, reads new. STANDS.
free ℓA
  // *** UNDERIVABLE *** — R-RETIRE requires Deed<… ⇒ ℓA> and Γ has none (S7); and
  // even with the deed, R-RETIRE's `_` admits retiring while s = I, discarding any
  // obligation the contents carry (S6).
read(p)                               // reject forever. STANDS.
```

**Revised verdict:** P7's substance — a hole made through one alias is visible
through the other, a fill through either restores both, free is permanent —
is the tuple's genuinely strong result and it survives. What does not survive
is the claim that the result is *structural*: the three rules that carry it
(`T-TAKE`, `T-PUT`, `T-REPL`) do not mention the pointer, and the rule that
would tie an access to an extent does not exist. The property is true of the
intended model and not of the written one.

### P9 — candidate says "accepted with a stated cost"; **overturned**

```text
fn drain<ℓx>(x: ptr<ℓx,T>, t: Pt<ℓx▷·,W,I>) -> (T, Pt<ℓx▷·,W,U>)
  // accept. STANDS — the hole is in the signature and the caller judges from it alone.
  //   This is R7's strongest clause under the tuple.
fn reserve<ℓv>(…) -> (Pt<ℓv▷·,W,I>, ∃ℓ'. Pt<ℓ'▷·,W,I> ⊗ Eq(backing(ℓv), ℓ'))
  // *** REJECT the clause *** — F6 above: Eq on location terms revives retired atoms,
  //   and it makes `backing(ℓv)` a flow-sensitive denotation, which §2.3 says the
  //   checker does not track and §2.7's type-level multiset equality cannot carry.
fn pick<ℓx,ℓy>(c, x, y) -> ∃ℓ ∈ {ℓx, ℓy}. ptr<ℓ,T>
match origin(r) { ℓx => write(r,1) with tx | ℓy => write(r,1) with ty }
  // accept HERE only because the two arms happen to erase to the same instruction.
  // The model states no obligation that they must:
  //   match origin(r) { ℓx => free(x) | ℓy => read(y) }
  // type-checks by the same rule, and after erasure (M6(iii)) it has no meaning,
  // because the origin is exactly what erasure removes (S5).
write(r, 1) without the match         // reject. STANDS.
```

**Revised verdict:** two of R7's three clauses (`drain`, `pick`) are carried
in one vocabulary as claimed. The third (`reserve`) is not: its stated form
is unsound, and the vocabulary it uses (`Eq`) is a fifth ghost form absent
from §2.1. The stated cost — "a two-arm erased ghost match" — omits the
obligation that makes an erased match meaningful at all.

### P13 — candidate says "accepted as required"; **overturned to violated**

```text
h = handle(i);  p = pointer_of(h) : ptr<slot(ℓP,i,g), Node>
pool.compact()  requires Pt<ℓP▷·,W,I> WHOLE
  // To obtain the whole-pool token the writer must R-RETIRE every carved slot.
  // R-RETIRE returns the parent extent at state **U** (F4), so the whole-pool token
  // the contract demands cannot be `I` unless some rule preserves state across
  // retirement — and no such rule exists.
  // *** the precondition is unsatisfiable as written ***
read(p)                               // reject. STANDS — but the reason given, "the
                                      //   current generation is g+1", is a fact about
                                      //   the term gen(P,i) at this program point,
                                      //   i.e. a flow-sensitive ghost environment the
                                      //   checker is said (§2.3) not to keep (F8).
read(pool[h])
  // *** REJECT *** — the candidate says accept.
  //   pool[h] "re-derives ptr<slot(ℓP,Fixup(h),g+1),Node> together with its token from
  //   Pt<ℓP▷·>".  The re-derivation is R-CARVE, and R-CARVE produces Pt<ℓ'▷·,W,**U**>.
  //   A read of a U slot is the step-0 hole read.  P13's required property — "the
  //   handle survives compaction" — therefore FAILS under the stated rules (F4).
p2 = fixup(Fixup, p)
  // *** REJECT *** — the candidate says accept, "erased; no runtime compare".
  //   compact() MOVED the object, so the correct p2 is a different address.
  //   Erased ⇒ p2 = p ⇒ read(p2) touches vacated storage: R1(ii)/R8a admitted with
  //   an accept comment (F5).
  //   Not erased ⇒ p2 is a lookup in a relocation table ⇒ bookkeeping state the
  //   source did not bind, refused by M2(ii) — the same clause that refuses a
  //   generational check, here wrapped as a ghost function.
```

**Revised verdict:** P13 is the program R8a's mutual-exclusion clause exists
for, and the candidate marks R8a **met** on the strength of it. Neither half
holds: the handle path rejects because carve yields `U`, and the fixup form
is unsound erased and M2(ii)-refused unerased. The honest reading is that
this tuple supports R8a's *prohibition* (no relocation while a token is
outstanding, enforced by the whole-extent precondition, which is a real and
attractive result) and supplies **no** fixup form, so R8a is partial, not met,
and P13's required property is unmet.

---

## 3. What survives

Stated so the findings are not read as a rejection of the tuple. Four results
are derived, not asserted, and no finding above touches them:

1. **P2's address-reuse refusal.** A retired atom plus a fresh atom for the
   reused bytes refuses the stale pointer at the type level, before any state
   is consulted. No other D1 family in the catalog does this as cheaply.
2. **P7's storage-indexed state.** Keying `⟨share, init⟩` to `ℓ▷e` and never
   to a pointer is exactly R1's P7 test, and the intended model passes it.
3. **P1's element-write overlap and its diagnostic.** `[i] ⊥ [j]` by the
   extent judgment, with `k ≠ i ∧ k ≠ j` as the literal missing-fact payload,
   is the strongest M7 payload of any candidate reviewed under this lens.
4. **R6's frame.** "A call can falsify only facts about extents whose tokens
   it received" is a structural frame with no kill rule, and the 34/41 `len()`
   rebind claim follows from it — subject to F8, which requires the length to
   be tracked somewhere, but not by the callee.

The findings concentrate in three places, and they are the same three places:
the rules that create and destroy locations (`R-CARVE`, `R-RETIRE`, and the
`Eq`/`gen`/`backing` terms that name them across such an event), the rules
that split and rejoin state (`R-REFINE`'s free `s`, `share`'s restore), and
the unstated bridge between a token's extent and the run-time values that
determine it (`len`, `cap`, the bump offset, the generation). W7 of the
candidate's own weakness list names the first of the three as the most likely
hole and declares the small-model check unrun; this critique finds that the
check is not needed to see it, and that the second and third are not on the
weakness list at all.

### What survives the lens

Three cost claims hold and should not be lost in the re-score.

- **E7's two largest measured writer taxes are genuinely removed.** The 120
  `region` blocks ("punctuation for the borrow checker") have no counterpart
  here, and the 34/41 `len()` rebinds lose their cause: a length in a sibling
  plane cannot be killed by an element write, and a callee's row names the
  extent rather than the whole parameter (R6). That is the strongest thing
  the candidate has.
- **P17's index arm is genuinely free.** `i ∈ run('V.data) = [0,len)` from the
  loop bound is a linear goal over the plane's own descriptor measure; no
  written step, no obligation on the element pointer. This is the one place
  the D1 refinement pays for itself against OPTIONS' warning that element
  identity makes "the proof burden arithmetic everywhere".
- **P7 needs no mechanism beyond D1+D3.** State on the storage rather than on
  the reference is derived, not asserted, and it is the test R9's negative
  clause exists for.

---

## 2. Program verdicts overturned

Notation follows the ladder.

### P6 — overturn **"accepted as required"** → **accepted with two costs priced at zero**

```text
out : O { bytes: plane<u8, len n> }
s = n / k                             // s is a VARIABLE, not a literal

par for w in 0..k
  writes out.bytes[w*s .. (w+1)*s)
{
  helper(split(out.bytes, w*s, (w+1)*s), input)
  // R5(a)(i) obligation: for w != w',
  //     disj( [w*s, (w+1)*s) , [w'*s, (w'+1)*s) )
  // i.e.  w+1 <= w'  &&  0 <= s   =>   (w+1)*s <= w'*s
  // reject under §2.1's named family: `w*s` is a product of two variables.
  //   Presburger has no such term, so the goal is not expressible in the
  //   "linear index fragment" §4.1 M1 names as the decider.          F1 / M1
  // accept only with a written step the candidate prices at 0:
  //   use (mul_mono: w+1 <= w' && 0 <= s => (w+1)*s <= w'*s);
  //   -> 1 lemma per partitioned loop                            M10 / M8
}

fn helper<'X,'I>(s: view<'X[lo..hi), u8>, inp: plane<'I, u8>)
    reads 'I  writes 's
{
  for j in lo..hi { s[j] = t(inp[j]) }
  // caller-side judgement from the signature alone:  ACCEPT, unchanged.  R7(e)
  // callee-side fact disj('X,'I):  REJECT — 'X and 'I are identity
  //   PARAMETERS; the carving that proves them distinct is in the caller,
  //   and §5 D6 forecloses "distinct by default, call-site proof".   S1 / R4(b)
  // consequence: no !alias.scope is derivable on these loads and stores;
  //   LLVM versions the loop exactly as rust-obvious did — 29 guards,
  //   2132 asm lines (E6).                                              M9
}
```

**New verdict.** P6's *interface* property (the caller judges from the
signature; `k` appears once) is upheld. P6's *cost* and *fact* properties are
not: one written nonlinear lemma per partitioned loop, and the alias fact the
candidate's home argument rests on is absent inside the callee. P5 keeps the
fact only because `Cols` is a nominal backing whose plane map is in the type;
the moment the callee is parameterized over identities, columns-first is where
Rust is.

### P13 — overturn **"accepted with a stated cost"** → the **accept** line is not derivable

```text
backing Pool { data: plane<Obj, len K, permutable>, map: ghost slot_of: atom -> index }
h = handle<'Pool#n>          // §2.2: "runtime: slot index"
p = elem<'Pool.data@e[slot_of(n)]>

pool.compact()               // permutes 'Pool.data; epoch e -> e+1; "map updated"
read(p)                      // reject: identity names @e, current epoch e+1.
                             //   UPHELD — this is a typing failure, ghost, free.
read(pool[h])                // candidate: accept, "resolved through the CURRENT map"
                             // reject as derived: §2.9 erases atoms and maps and
                             //   leaves "base pointers, lengths, INDICES", so the
                             //   erased program holds the pre-compaction slot and
                             //   reads the wrong occupant in bounds — the exact
                             //   hazard §3 P3 introduced the atom to refuse.  F2
```

The accept line is true only under one of three run-time mechanisms, each of
which contradicts a claim the candidate makes:

| Mechanism | What it costs | What it breaks |
|---|---|---|
| (i) `compact` rewrites the index inside every live handle | a write per live handle per compaction | §5 D8 **forecloses** the runtime-rewriting fixup; bookkeeping the source did not bind — **M2(ii)** |
| (ii) a real `atom → index` table every `pool[h]` loads through | one dependent load per handle access, plus a plane | §2.9's erasure claim; §4.3 prices it at 0; the map is **data**, not ghost |
| (iii) `h` stores the atom, `pool[h]` searches | not constant time | M9's floor |

**New verdict.** P13 is **accepted only under (ii), with the map as ordinary
writer-written data**: one extra plane, one written invariant relating `map` to
occupancy, and one dependent load per handle access — a cost §4.3's "one ghost
atom per occupant type + one plane-level invariant" does not contain. The
*rejection* half of P13 (the ghost epoch refusing the stale `elem`) is upheld
and is genuinely free; only the *fixup channel* R8a demands is mispriced.

### P16 — overturn **"the `Cols<E>` and closure cases are accepted with a stated cost"**

```text
let h = |s: view<'X[lo..hi)>| helper(s, input)
// accept HERE ONLY: h is applied at its binding site, so 'I is a concrete plane.

fs = [ |s| helper(s, inputA) , |s| helper(s, inputB) ]
// reject: the two closure types carry different capture rows ('IA vs 'IB);
//   they have no common type, so `plane<F>` of them does not type.      R15(a)

fn run_all<F>(fs: plane<F>, out: plane<'O,u8>)
// reject: F's capture row is a row of unknown length over unknown planes —
//   the SAME row variable over a plane list §3 P16 says only the generic
//   pool needs.                                                          S5
```

**New verdict.** **Two of P16's four sub-programs** need the unbuilt D7
mechanism, not one. P6-through-a-closure is first-order only in the immediate
-application shape; a stored or higher-order closure is the generic-pool
problem wearing a lambda. `Cols<E>` and `pick<N: Nominal>` stand. This matters
for R15 because the candidate's honest weakness 7 localizes the gap to
"generics over plane lists", when it is "generics over plane lists **and every
first-class closure**".

### P4 — overturn **"accepted with a stated cost (1 parameter)"** → the stated repair does not type

```text
struct Cursor<'B.c> { at: plane<'B.c, u64>, i: usize }
c = Cursor { at: v.data, i: 0 }                 // c : Cursor<'V.data>

if len(v) < cap(v) { push(v,5); b = c.read() }  // c : Cursor<'V.data>
else { push(v,5); c = Cursor { at: v.data, i: c.i } }
                                                // §2.5: push's else-arm yields a
                                                //   FRESH backing, so here
                                                //   c : Cursor<'V'.data>
free(v); c.read()
// reject: at the join `c` has two types. HIS-D1-14's finite origin set is
//   stated in §2.7 and P9 for CALL RESULTS only, never for a struct's type
//   ARGUMENT at a branch join.                                    S8 / R15
```

**New verdict.** P4 is **accepted with a further needed mechanism**: origin
sets must be admissible as type-constructor arguments with a stated join rule
(`Cursor<{'V.data,'V'.data}>`), or the candidate must state that a struct
holding an identity cannot be rebound across a reallocating branch — in which
case P4's own required property ("a stored pointer or handle to a container in
a struct; validity decided by state and proof") is only half met. The claim the
candidate is right to make — that **`push` is never blocked by the cursor's
existence** — is untouched and is a real win over every borrow-based family.

### P1 — overturn **"accepted as required"** → accepted; the family that decides it is specified only for the derived case

```text
pi = split_one(v.data, i); pj = split_one(v.data, j); pw = split_one(v.data, w)
par { write(pi,x); write(pj,y); write(pw,z) }
// needs i!=j, i!=w, j!=w  -- pairwise, O(s^2) in live split sites.    M10

read(v.data[k])    // residue = [0,n) \ ([i,i+1) u [j,j+1) u [w,w+1))
                   // accept iff k!=i && k!=j && k!=w   -- MEMBERSHIP, O(s),
                   //   and this is the only case §3 P1 derives.

q = split_range(v.data, lo, hi)
// needs disj([lo,hi), residue): [lo,hi) must be inside [0,n) and miss each
//   hole. lo, hi, i, j, w are symbolic and only PARTIALLY ordered, so the
//   procedure must enumerate endpoint orderings (exponential in s) or
//   reject when unsure. The candidate states neither.           S7 / M1(b)
push(v, x)         // reject while any split is live: "'V.data is split at ..."
```

**New verdict.** P1's derived lines are accepted and its diagnostic payload
(`k != i && k != j`) is a genuine M7 win over `OWN-6`'s coordinate-only
rejection (E7). But the split algebra §2.5 introduces is specified only for
hole-membership; residue-versus-extent disjointness — which P1 reaches with one
more line — has neither a decision procedure nor an M10 degree.

### P2 — overturn **"accepted with a stated cost (one invariant, ~6 steps)"**

```text
b1 = alloc(A, 64)?   // reject as written: owner decision 5 (settled, interim (b))
b2 = alloc(A, 64)?   //   puts allocation failure OUTSIDE the outcome model, in
b3 = alloc(A, 64)?   //   R14(v). §4.1's own R12 row says so; the derivation uses
                     //   the refused spelling anyway.                     S10

free(A, b2); b4 = alloc(A, 32)
// accept requires: b4's extent is disjoint from b1, b3 and from every other
//   live issued extent. Not split arithmetic — the arena's free-list invariant.
// cost as stated: "~6 use steps".
// cost as measured: the invariant is an inequality CONTEXT over the endpoints
//   of every live extent, which is the `growing` shape of E3 — N=16 30 ms,
//   N=32 165 ms, N=64 1691 ms — and E4 shows the driver is context size, not
//   the six written steps. Premise count grows with live extents.        S11
read(b2[0])          // reject: R1(ii), identity Gone. UPHELD and free.
```

**New verdict.** P2 is **accepted with a cost that is a function of live
extents, not a constant six steps**, and its derivation must be rewritten
without `?` under decision 5. The half the candidate gets right — that address
reuse mints a fresh identity, so the stale pointer is refused by identity
rather than by a generation compare — stands, and is the cleanest M2(ii)
result in the candidate.

### P5 — overturn **"accepted as required"** → **accepted with a stated cost**

```text
backing Cols { a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h : plane<u64, len n, align 64> }

for i in 0..n
  writes Cols.a[i], Cols.b[i]                          // 8 identities named in
  reads  Cols.c[i],Cols.d[i],Cols.e[i],Cols.f[i],      //   the row, restated at
         Cols.g[i],Cols.h[i]                           //   every such loop  S13
{ ... }
// alias facts: ACCEPT and FREE — 8 planes pairwise disjoint by the plane map,
//   which the writer wrote as the layout. UPHELD; this is the candidate's
//   home case and it holds.
// PAR-2 overlap: accept only WITH the row. Omit the row and M5's chosen
//   degradation leaves the loop sequential-and-accepted, so the obvious
//   shape is the fast shape for the ALIAS channel and the slow shape for
//   the PARALLEL one.                                                    S13
// the cited measurement: E6 is 0 guards and 17x code size at PARITY time,
//   with the time delta short-trip only (n=8: 2.0x; parity n>=32), and its
//   derivation was OWN-1 affinity + OWN-5 &uniq — mechanisms §1 D4 retires.
//   The plane map re-derives the per-plane scopes; it does not re-derive
//   the parameter noalias or the shared-borrow class.                    S12
```

**New verdict.** P5 is accepted and is the candidate's strongest case, but not
"as required" at zero cost: one clause per touched identity per loop, and the
quoted evidence supports *code size and short trips*, not a general speed
claim. The sentence "the obvious shape **is** the declared shape" is true of
the plane map and false of the access row.

# Critique: columns-first — lens SOUNDNESS AND THE PROGRAMS

Refutation date: 2026-09-16. Target:
[candidate-columns-first.md](candidate-columns-first.md). Lens: re-derive P1, P2,
P4, P7, P9, P13 against the candidate **as written** (§2's model text is the
authority, not §3's prose), and report every wrong accept/reject, every R1–R3 /
R11 / R12 hazard that slips through, every M2(ii) violation hidden as data or as
a typed outcome, every fact the candidate uses without saying where it comes
from, and every coupling C1–C18 it retunes without saying so.

Method note: where §3 and §2 disagree, §2 wins, because §2 is what a checker
would implement. Three of the seven fatal findings are exactly of that shape —
the prose derivation reaches the right verdict by a rule the model does not
contain.

---

## 1. Findings

Severity: **fatal** = a hazard is admitted or a requirement is violated in a way
the candidate did not declare; **serious** = a program verdict is wrong, a
stated cost is understated, or a needed mechanism is unnamed; **minor** =
wording.

| # | Sev | Program / requirement | Finding | One-sentence fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | fatal | R6, M6(ii), C2; P7, P11, P1 | §2.3's kill rule — "a write to `u` kills facts whose support is `u` or a descendant of `u`, **and nothing else**" — under-kills in two directions: a write to `'B.c[i]` with symbolic `i` does not kill a fact supported by the *sibling* `'B.c[j]` when `i ≠ j` is unproved, and does not kill a fact supported by the *ancestor* `'B.c` (e.g. "every element of `'B.c` is < 10"). M6(ii) says a design whose frame under-kills fails P7/P2; R6 is declared **met** and M6 declared partial for unrelated reasons. | Restate the kill as "kills every fact whose support is not **proved disjoint** from `u`", i.e. the may-write over-approximation C2 demands, and keep `disj` for the R4/R5 direction only. |
| F2 | fatal | R1(ii), R2; P2 | §2.3 gives state only to backings (`Live \| Gone`) and to planes (`run, punct, epoch`), and defines `Gone('B.c)` **iff** `state('B) = Gone`. An extent has no state. So after `free(A, b2)`, `'A` is still `Live` and `read(b2[0])` is **accepted**: P2's central negative test (a pointer into `b2` refused after `b4` reuses its bytes) fails, and `free(A,b2); free(A,b2)` is refused by nothing, since §2.2 makes every descriptor copyable and no affine owner exists for a block. | Add a per-extent liveness axis to §2.3 (a finite set of retired sub-extents per plane) and price it — it is a third state axis, not a refinement of `run`. |
| F3 | fatal | R4, R5(a)(i), C2, C3, M1; P2 | §2.1 defines `disj` with an **iff** over four cases (plane map, different backings, half-open arithmetic, proved `i ≠ j`). `b1`, `b2`, `b3` are existential extents at opaque offsets `o1, o2, o3`; no arithmetic relates them, so none of the four cases applies and the `par { fill(b1); fill(b2); fill(b3) }` accept is not derivable. §3's reason — "pairwise disj by the arena invariant" — is a fifth source of `disj`: instantiating a writer-stated quantified invariant over a free list. That is exactly the channel C2 says must be stated once and C3 warns is unsound when it is not discharged per pair, and quantifier instantiation inside an automatic family is an M1 hazard. | State the invariant channel explicitly as a fifth `disj` clause with its instantiation rule fixed (which quantified premises, at which sites), or overturn P2's `par` accept. |
| F4 | fatal | R4, R5(a)(i), R6; P9 | D1 adopts HIS-D1-14 origin sets and P9 gives `pick` the result type `elem<{'X,'Y}>`, but §2.1's `ident` grammar has no production for a set and `disj` is defined only over single tree nodes. Under the written rule, `{'X,'Y}` is neither a descendant of `'X` nor an ancestor of it, so `par { write(r, 1); write(px, 2) }` is **accepted** — a data race and a false licensed fact. The kill direction is equally undefined: a write through `r` must kill the union over both origins, while §2.3 keys kills to one node. | Define footprint containment over origin sets ("overlaps iff it overlaps some member") in §2.1 and make the kill the union over members; add the set production to the grammar. |
| F5 | fatal | R1, R8a, M2(ii), M9; P13 | §2.2 gives `handle<'B.c#n, T>` the runtime representation "slot index", and §2.9 erases the `slot_of` map ("map: **ghost**"). After `pool.compact()` the object has moved, so `read(pool[h])` reads the pre-compaction slot: the accept is wrong. The only repair is a materialized atom→index table that `compact` rewrites — real runtime data, a real indirection and a real maintenance cost, all unpriced, and §5's D8 row explicitly forecloses it ("nothing rewrites a stored pointer"). | Make the map ordinary data (a plane of the pool), say so in §2.2, §2.9 and §5's D8 row, and charge the indirection to M9 and the table write to `compact`'s row. |
| F6 | fatal | M1, R1(ii), R2, C6; P8, P4, P9 | §2.6 says that beyond the atom bound `k` "the join takes the meet", but §2.3's `state('B) ::= Live \| Gone` is a two-point **flat** set with no order, no meet and no `Unknown`. Acceptance at that point is undefined, so M1's "acceptance is a total function of the source" is not met; and no single choice is conservative for both R1 and R2 at once (assuming `Live` admits use-after-free, assuming `Gone` turns a required `free` into a double free). | Give the state a proper lattice with a top element that rejects both reads and `free` (over-rejection, not a wrong accept), and state the direction separately for R1 facts and R2 obligations. |
| F7 | fatal | R1(i), R7, M1; P9, P7, P8 | §2.5's `take` unconditionally does `punct ∪= {i}`, and **no row in §2.5 ever reaches `run = Empty`** or converts punctures into a shrunken run. Two consequences: (a) a loop that takes without putting at one textual site produces `n` holes while §2.3 bounds `\|punct\|` by the number of textual take sites, and no behavior at the bound is stated — the natural reading (drop an entry) is an R1(i) hole read; (b) `drain`'s body in P9, whose contract is `exit run('X) = Empty`, is therefore **not expressible**, so R7's "every accepted callee body satisfies its interface" fails while R7 is declared met. | Add a `take` variant that retracts the run at its end (and an `Empty`-reaching rule), and state the behavior at the `\|punct\|` bound as a rejection with a named diagnostic, never as a dropped entry. |
| S1 | serious | R1(i), R11; P1 | The line `if k != i && k != j { read(v.data[k]) } // accept` is wrong: `k` is a runtime index and `k < n` is nowhere established. The candidate's own P17 rejects the identical shape ("k a runtime value: reject, needs k < len(v.data)"). | Rewrite the P1 line as accepted only under `k < n && k != i && k != j`, and say the residue covers `k` *given* the bound. |
| S2 | serious | R1(i); P4 | `a = c.read() // accept: run('V.data) = [0,len) and i < len` — `i = 0` and `len` is a runtime value, so `0 < len` is unprovable (the vector may be empty); and for the stored-cursor reads the fact `c.i < len(v)` relates the contents of two separate storages across a struct boundary, which §2.7's signature vocabulary (entry/exit state, footprints, existentials, origin sets, outcomes, resource effects — "nothing else") cannot state. | Add a struct-invariant (refinement) form to §2.7 and charge it, and make P4's first read conditional on a written `len(v) > 0`. |
| S3 | serious | R8a, R15; P4 | The `else` arm `{ push(v,5); c = Cursor { at: v.data, i: c.i } }` does not type: `Cursor<'B.c>` carries the identity as a **type parameter**, so the then-arm leaves `c : Cursor<'V.data>` and the else-arm leaves `c : Cursor<'V'.data>` where `'V'` is an existential unpacked inside that arm. The join has no type for `c`, and the later `free(v)` and `c.read()` lines need one. R8a is declared **met** although its own red clause is conditional reallocation — this line. | Either let the joined identity be an origin set (and then F4 must be fixed first), or state a rebinding rule that re-opens the existential at the join and charge it to R8a. |
| S4 | serious | C4, C8, C9; P1, P4, P9 | `&V` (P9 `reserve`), `v` in `push(v,x)`, `free(v)`, `alloc(A,n)`, `pool.compact()` all pass or name a **whole backing**, but §2.2 defines exactly three reference forms plus `handle`, none of which names a backing. How a multi-plane aggregate is passed, and what identity a parameter of backing type carries, is never stated. | Add a `backing<'B>` descriptor form to §2.2 with its row semantics (it names every plane of `'B`), or state that a backing parameter desugars to one identity parameter per plane and re-derive R15's parameter count. |
| S5 | serious | R7, C6, M10; P9, P4 | `reserve`'s exit `ite(cap0 >= m, ...)` and `push`'s `ite(len0 < cap0, ...)` name **pre-state contents** of planes the same call writes. §2.6 says an atom is "a pure boolean the writer bound"; a two-state (`old(cap)`) contract vocabulary is a different mechanism and is never named, and the fact it depends on is killed by the very call that states it. | Name the two-state contract vocabulary in §2.6 (entry-value atoms and their capture rule), and price it against M8/M10. |
| S6 | serious | R12, M2(i), C15; P2 | P2 writes `b1 = alloc(A, 64)?`, i.e. a typed allocation-failure outcome, which is owner decision 5 option (a); the settled interim is (b) — abort with a record, outside the outcome model — and the candidate's own §4.1 R12 row says so. So M2 is declared **met** while P2's accepted program carries an abort edge the candidate leaves unaccounted, and P18's "R2 holds on every failure arm" is never derived. | Drop the `?` from P2 and state the abort edge under R14(v), or keep the `?` and declare M2(i) violated pending owner decision 5. |
| S7 | serious | M2(ii), R1(ii); §2.4, P3 (bearing on P11 and P2) | §2.4 promises a bit may never discharge an R1 obligation, and P11 honors it. P3's traverse does not: `read(data[cur])` needs `cur < K` and "atom(cur) is not retired" (P3 itself makes a retired atom an R1(ii) rejection), and both are reachable only from the invariant `forall s in **occupied**(Pool): atom(next[s]) in atoms(Pool)` — whose runtime witness at `cur` is the `live` bit. The bit therefore discharges an R1(ii)/bound obligation: an M2(ii) violation hidden as ordinary data. | Either strengthen the invariant to hold at every slot (making `live` genuinely semantic), or state that a link-followed traverse is rejected without a written `use` step, and re-derive P3's cost. |
| S8 | serious | C14, M4; P1, §6.8 | §2.2 states that references carry "no permission and **no duration**", yet §6.8 concedes that a split's children "may not be stored". An escape restriction on a value's type is a duration by another name, it is a second axis §2.2 denies, and it answers C14's loan-channel question silently. §3's objection-answer (c) rests on the denial. | State the escape rule as an explicit scoping construct in §2.5's `split` row, and record in §6 that the candidate re-introduces one scoped axis rather than none. |

| S14 | serious | M6(i), M10, D13 | "Per plane the state space is (4 run shapes x bounded punctures x epoch)" and D13's "unusually cheap" bounded check are understated once F2's per-extent liveness is added: the retired-sub-extent set grows with the number of `free` calls and is not bounded by anything syntactic. | Re-state the per-plane state space with the liveness axis and re-cost M6(i) and M10. |
| m1 | minor | P13 | §2.1's grammar generates `'B.c@e` or `'B.c[i]`, never the `'Pool.data@e[slot_of(n)]` P13 uses; as generated, an `elem` carries no epoch, so §2.5's "epoch current" precondition has nothing to read. | Add the `'B.c@e[i]` production. |
| m2 | minor | P13 | `map: ghost slot-of : atom -> index` sits inside a plane map that §2.1 defines as the *layout* and part of the type; a ghost member is a construct the grammar does not admit. | Declare the map as an attribute of the plane, not a member of the plane map. |
| m3 | minor | P1 | `split_one` carves one element out of the middle (a three-way carve) and is then applied to an already-split parent; §2.5 defines only two-way `split(view, at)`. | Add the three-way carve and the residue-split rule to §2.5, or spell P1 with two `split`s. |
| m4 | minor | P1, P6 | §2.5 defines `read`/`write` for `elem` only; P1 and P6 write through views. | Add a view write row with its footprint. |
| m5 | minor | M4 | `free(A, b)` and `free('B)` are two spellings of one construct with different preconditions — an M4 instance the candidate's §6.2 list of three does not include. | Add it to §6.2's list. |
| m6 | minor | R2 | §2.5's `free('B)` row lists no `Live('B)` precondition, so `free(v); free(v)` is refused by nothing written. | Add `Live('B)` to the precondition. |
| m7 | minor | §4.1 | The stated counts are wrong: the table has 16 met, 10 partial, 1 violated, not "met 17, partial 9, violated 1". | Correct the counts. |

### Couplings retuned without saying so

- **C2** (one distinctness relation, two exactness directions) — retuned twice: F1 states only the R4 direction and uses it for frame, and F3 adds a second source of `disj` outside its own `iff`.
- **C3** (distinct-by-default with call-site discharge) — F3's arena-invariant channel is the form C3 says is sound only if every call site discharges every pair, sub-identities included; no call-site obligation is stated.
- **C1** (one identity granularity serving state, distinctness, footprints and kills) — broken by F2: the granularity at which `disj` and footprints work (extents) is finer than the granularity at which liveness state exists (backings).
- **C6** (state as a term over captured conditions) — F6: the definiteness rule that "replaces drop flags" is undefined at the `k` bound.
- **C14** (the loan channel) — S8 answers it by an unstated escape restriction.
- **C15** (outcome arms multiply R2's join paths) — S6: the `?` in P2 is written and its arms never derived.
- **C10** (read-only interface as a type flag, never a loan) — silently dropped: §2.2 puts no flag on any reference, so read-only-ness exists only in a row, and a stored `plane<'B.c,T>` in a struct carries no read-only fact at all.

---

## 2. Program verdicts overturned

### P1 — "accepted as required" → **accepted, with one line of the derivation overturned**

```text
v : V { data: plane<u64, len n>, len: plane<usize,1> }
pi = split_one(v.data, i)          // accept (with i < n)      -- but see m3: a 3-way carve
pj = split_one(v.data, j)          // accept iff i != j AND j < n
par { write(pi,x) ; write(pj,y) }  // accept: disj by index fragment      R5(a)(i)
k = f(...)
read(v.data[k])                    // reject: needs k < n && k != i && k != j
if k != i && k != j {
  read(v.data[k])                  // REJECT  <- candidate says accept
}                                  //   k < n is nowhere established; run('V.data) = [0,n)
                                   //   and R1(i) needs k ∈ run. The candidate's own P17
                                   //   rejects this exact shape.                   [S1]
if k < n && k != i && k != j {
  read(v.data[k])                  // accept: residue covers k, bound from the writer's test
}
join pi, pj ; push(v, x)           // accept
```
P1's requirements still hold, but the diagnostic the row demands must name
`k < n` as well, and F1 applies to any *contents* fact about `v.data[k]` carried
across `write(pi,x)`: with `i` symbolic the stated kill rule leaves it standing.

### P2 — "accepted with a stated cost" → **as written, admits use-after-free and does not prove its overlap**

```text
backing A { meta: plane<Hdr>, bytes: plane<u8, len N> }
b1 = alloc(A,64)?  b2 = alloc(A,64)?  b3 = alloc(A,64)?
                   // `?` presumes a typed allocation outcome; owner decision 5 (b) says
                   //   otherwise, and §4.1's own R12 row agrees.                    [S6]
par { fill(b1); fill(b2); fill(b3) }
                   // NOT DERIVABLE: o1,o2,o3 are opaque existentials; §2.1's disj is an
                   //   `iff` over four cases and none applies. The arena invariant is a
                   //   fifth source the model never declares.                       [F3]
free(A, b2)        // accept
b4 = alloc(A, 32)  // accept
read(b2[0])        // ACCEPT  <- candidate says reject
                   //   §2.3: Gone('B.c) iff state('B) = Gone. 'A is Live. An extent has
                   //   no state at all, so nothing in the model refuses this read.  [F2]
free(A, b2)        // ACCEPT  <- nothing refuses a double free: descriptors are copyable
                   //   (§2.2) and no affine owner exists for a block.               [F2]
```
P2 is the row that R1(ii), R2 and R4(e) are all tested on, and the candidate
fails all three under its own §2 text while declaring R1, R2 and R4 **met**.
The §3 prose reaches the right verdicts; the model does not contain the rules
that would produce them.

### P4 — "accepted with a stated cost" → **not accepted: the repair does not type**

```text
struct Cursor<'B.c> { at: plane<'B.c,u64>, i: usize }
c = Cursor { at: v.data, i: 0 }
a = c.read()        // REJECT  <- candidate says accept: 0 < len is unprovable for an
                    //   empty vector, and `c.i < len(v)` is a cross-storage refinement
                    //   §2.7 cannot state.                                          [S2]
push(v, 5)          // exit ite(len0 < cap0, 'V unchanged, 'V Gone ∧ fresh 'V)
                    //   `len0`, `cap0` are pre-state contents atoms §2.6 has no
                    //   vocabulary for.                                             [S5]
b = c.read()        // reject unless len0 < cap0                       (agreed)
if len(v) < cap(v) { push(v,5); b = c.read() }        // accept        (agreed)
else { push(v,5); c = Cursor { at: v.data, i: c.i } } // ILL-TYPED  <- candidate says accept
                    //   then-arm: c : Cursor<'V.data>;  else-arm: c : Cursor<'V'.data>
                    //   with 'V' existentially unpacked inside the arm. The join has no
                    //   type for c, and free(v) / c.read() below need one.           [S3]
free(v)             // accept (but §2.5 states no Live precondition)                 [m6]
c.read()            // reject forever                                  (agreed)
```
P4's requirement is "validity decided by state and proof, not by a borrow that
blocks push". The candidate does not block `push` — that half is genuinely won —
but it cannot **carry the cursor past the reallocating arm**, which is the other
half of the same requirement. R8a is declared met; on this program it is red,
exactly as VERDICT-D0's R8a status line already says.

### P7 — "accepted as required" → **one line overturned; the rest stands**

```text
p = elem<'A.v[0]>  ;  q = elem<'A.v[0]>
x = take(p)         // accept; punct = {0}                             (agreed)
read(q)             // reject: 0 ∈ punct                               (agreed — this is
                    //   the candidate's best result: state on the storage, not the pointer)
put(q, move x)      // accept; punct = ∅                               (agreed)
read(p)             // accept                                          (agreed)
old = replace(p,new)// accept                                          (agreed)
read(q)             // accept: reads `new`                             (agreed)
free(A)             // REJECT  <- candidate says accept
                    //   §2.5's free('B) needs "every plane Empty of affine elements".
                    //   replace returned `old` and LEFT `new` in the slot; run = [0,1).
                    //   Neither `new` nor `old` has an obligation discharged, and §2.5
                    //   has no release row for an affine local at all.               [S11]
read(p)             // reject forever                                  (agreed)
```
Note also that P7 works only because `p` and `q` name the *same* node. Change it
to `p = elem<'A.v[i]>`, `q = elem<'A.v[j]>` with `i`, `j` symbolic, and F1 bites:
`write(p, 5)` leaves a contents fact about `q` standing.

### P9 — "accepted with a stated cost" → **`drain` is unwritable and `pick`'s result is unsound in parallel**

```text
fn drain<'X>(x: plane<'X,T>) writes 'X entry run('X)=[0,len) exit run('X)=Empty
                    // BODY NOT EXPRESSIBLE: §2.5 has no transition reaching run = Empty,
                    //   and `take` only punctures; a loop of takes exceeds
                    //   |punct| <= textual take sites with no stated behavior at the
                    //   bound. R7 requires every accepted body to satisfy its interface. [F7]
reserve(v, 100)     // accept only with a two-state contract vocabulary (old(cap))     [S5]
r = pick(c, px, py) // r : elem<{'X,'Y}> — a form §2.1's grammar does not generate
write(r)            // sequentially: "facts true of both origins" is right, but the KILL
                    //   is undefined (§2.3 keys kills to one node).                   [F4]
par { write(r,1) ; write(px,2) }
                    // ACCEPT under the written disj  <- must REJECT.
                    //   {'X,'Y} is neither ancestor nor descendant of 'X, and 'X and 'Y
                    //   are different backings, so the four disj cases yield "disjoint".
                    //   A data race is admitted and a false R4 fact is licensed.       [F4]
if c { write(px) } else { write(py) }   // accept                       (agreed)
```

### P13 — "accepted with a stated cost" → **the fixup form does not exist at run time**

```text
backing Pool { data: plane<Obj, len K, permutable>, map: ghost slot_of: atom -> index }
h = handle<'Pool#n>                  // runtime: a slot index (§2.2)
p = elem<'Pool.data@e[slot_of(n)]>   // a form the grammar does not generate            [m1]
pool.compact()                       // permutes 'Pool.data; epoch e -> e+1
read(p)                              // reject: stale epoch                (agreed — and
                                     //   correctly a typing failure, with no runtime compare)
read(pool[h])                        // REJECT  <- candidate says accept.
                                     //   h's runtime value is the OLD slot index and the
                                     //   map is ghost (§2.9 erases atoms and epochs), so
                                     //   there is nothing at run time to resolve through:
                                     //   the read lands on the pre-compaction slot and
                                     //   returns a different object. Making the map real
                                     //   data contradicts §5's D8 row ("nothing rewrites a
                                     //   stored pointer") and adds an unpriced indirection
                                     //   plus a table write inside compact.             [F5]
```
P13's requirement is that a **contract-visible fixup form** exists. The epoch
supplies the *invalidation* half correctly and cheaply; the handle does not
supply the *survival* half, because a ghost map cannot redirect a runtime index.
Either the map becomes ordinary data — in which case P13 is accepted at a stated
runtime cost that §4.3 and §6 must both carry — or P13 is refused and the
candidate's answer to R8a is "invalidate everything, fix up nothing".

---

## 3. What survives

The findings above are repairs, not a refutation of the tuple. What the lens
confirms as genuinely won:

- **P7's core** (state on the storage; a hole made through `p` visible through
  `q`; `free` permanent) is exact and needs no mechanism beyond D1+D3, as
  claimed — for coinciding, *syntactically equal* identities.
- **P5 and P6** are not re-derived here, but nothing in the findings touches
  them: the plane map gives distinctness with no proof, and half-open worker
  slices are in the index fragment.
- **P4's non-blocking `push`** is real and is the thing a borrow-based candidate
  cannot do. The failure is the join after the reallocating arm, not the push.
- **P13's invalidation** by ghost epoch is a clean M2-respecting `reject`, with
  no runtime compare.

The pattern of the seven fatal findings is one thing: §2's model is written for
the *homogeneous, statically carved, syntactically named* case (P5, P6, P7's
single slot), and every program that carves **dynamically** (P2), names a
**joined or set-valued** identity (P9, P4), or needs a **runtime survivor**
across a layout change (P13) reaches its stated verdict through a rule the model
does not contain.

# Critique of candidate-generational-handles — lens COST, DETERMINISM, WRITER

Research date: 2026-09-16. Refuter lens: M1 (fixed terminating procedure, no
search or budget), M10 (degree in program size and written steps; edit reach),
M7 (locally repairable rejection), M8 (spec-token count of the vocabulary),
M9 (P5/P6 obvious shape; surviving backend facts), R15 (generics, closures,
nominals without signature explosion). Target:
[candidate-generational-handles.md](candidate-generational-handles.md).
Grounding: VERDICT-D0 §2 (rows), §4 (couplings), §5 (premises), §7 (owner
interims), MECHANISM-MAP §3 (ladder), PROGRAMS.md (P1–P19),
EVIDENCE-mechanism-survey part B, and the measured series in the repository
(`research/experiments/proof-use-cost`,
`research/experiments/scoped-alias-channel/RESULTS.md`,
`research/experiments/blind-writer/2026-08-28`).

The candidate's headline honesty statement concedes Tier B and asks to be
judged on Tier A. This critique judges Tier A only. Tier B is not attacked
anywhere below; every finding lands inside the tier the candidate says it
stands on.

Severity, as the task defines it: **fatal** = a hazard is admitted, or a
requirement is violated in a way the candidate did not declare; **serious** =
a program verdict is wrong, a stated cost is understated, or a needed
mechanism is unnamed; **minor** = wording.

---

## 1. Findings

| # | Sev | Program / requirement | Finding | One-sentence fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | **fatal** | P5; R4(a) soundness, R4 declared **met**; M6(iii); M9 | P5's eight columns are `buffer<u64>` **fields**, and the candidate derives their element disjointness from "distinct FIELD PATHS of one root are disjoint by construction". Field paths `'c.a` and `'c.c` are disjoint; their **backings** are not. §2.1 gives every container a separate `backing('v) = 'b`, and D4's base stance ("unrestricted aliasing, safety from per-storage state") explicitly drops the two mechanisms — OWN-1 affinity of `buffer<T>` and OWN-5 exclusivity — that make two live buffer values non-overlapping today. Under this tuple `Cols { a: b0, c: b0, … }` is a constructible value, so the per-load fact the candidate licenses to lowering is false in an execution R14's model admits. | State a written `Cols`-level invariant `pairwise-disjoint(backing(a)…backing(h))` discharged at construction and carried as a bound on `kernel`, and re-charge P5 with its 28 pairwise facts. |
| F2 | **fatal** | P1, P3, P5, P11; M1 declared **met**, M1(b) | The candidate names exactly four automatic families (literal-conjunction entailment, affine normalisation, lattice-height fixpoint, syntactic instantiation of written steps) and then uses a fifth in three derivations: whole-container quantified state (`state('c.a[i]) = Init` for symbolic `i`, "whole-buffer Init"), `push`'s `requires state('b[i]) = Init for all i<n`, the wildcard footprint `writes 'G[*].data`, and `take2`'s weakening of a universal to "all except two". Maintaining a quantified array fact across a symbolic-index write is the array/quantifier domain; M1(b) demands each family be given as a decision procedure with a stated bound, and none is given. | Name the array-state family with its degree, or require a written `invariant` for every whole-container state fact and re-charge P1's and P5's writer cost from 0. |
| F3 | **fatal** | P2 in loop form, P18; M1 declared **met**, M10; R2 declared **met** | §2.5's loop-head rule demands a clause only for (a) a place whose state the body changes and (b) each pool the body frees into, for liveness facts used after the free. A loop that only **allocates** matches neither, yet each iteration adds a fresh ghost `σ` to `Live(P)` and each `free` produces a new `succ(γ)` term. `Live(P)`, `Gen` (a symbolic successor term, §2.4 rule 2, deliberately unbounded) and the existential backing names of §2.4's `grow` are all infinite-height domains, so "the fixpoint terminates by lattice height" is not established, and no widening is stated. The same gap sits on branch atoms across a back edge: §2.5's atoms are branch literals with no stated versioning, so `if stop { break }` with a loop-carried `stop` has no defined atom identity at the head. As written, either the pool body carries an unproved partial operation (R11) or the lowering carries a failure edge absent from source (M2(i)). | Give `alloc` a stated domain (`\|Live(P)\| < N` plus a free-list/occupancy invariant) or a written outcome arm, and derive P18 against it. |
